The Baal Cycle

Wheel of Heaven Translation

The Late Bronze Age Northwest-Semitic storm-god mythological cycle from Ras Shamra (ancient Ugarit, modern Latakia, Syria) — six tablets recovered 1929–1931, narrating Baʿlu's conflicts with Yammu (Sea) and Môtu (Death) and his ascension to kingship over the gods. THE primary comparative-mythology nexus for the Hebrew Bible: Yahweh-vs-Yam (Ps 74, 89, 93; Isa 27:1), El/Elohim, bnei elohim, Asherah, Leviathan/Lôtanu, mavet/Môtu, the storm-theophany at Sinai.

Direct Direct Established or uncontested across mainstream sources, or a direct description of the project itself. Framework Framework Foundational premise of the Wheel of Heaven framework. Explicit in the Raëlian canon; not endorsed by mainstream scholarship. Inferred Inferred A reasonable reading of comparative material — not stated literally, but consistent with the source. Speculative Speculative Interpretive synthesis or hypothesis that goes beyond what any single source states.

An English translation of the Ugaritic Baal Cycle, produced from a best-effort reconstruction of the alphabetic-cuneiform text based on named scholarly editions (verification pending against KTU³ Dietrich-Loretz-Sanmartín 2013). **The project's first Ugaritic-source text and first Levantine-tradition text.** The Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6) is preserved on six clay tablets discovered at the royal palace of Ugarit (Ras Shamra) in the 1929–1931 excavations led by Claude Schaeffer. The tablets are scribed in the Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform script (a 30-letter Northwest-Semitic abjad rendered with cuneiform-shaped wedges on clay — distinct from the syllabic Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform of Mesopotamia). The cycle was likely composed in the 14th–13th centuries BCE. The six-tablet narrative covers: (i) the conflict with Yammu / Sea (KTU 1.1 + 1.2 — chapter 1 of this translation), in which Baʿlu defeats the chaos-monster sea-god; (ii) Baʿlu's palace-building on Mount Ṣapunu (KTU 1.3 + 1.4); (iii) the conflict with Môtu / Death (KTU 1.5 + 1.6), in which Baʿlu is swallowed by Death, his sister Anat ritually destroys Mot, and Baʿlu returns to life. The cycle is the most extensively-preserved Late Bronze Age mythological composition from anywhere in the eastern Mediterranean and is the central comparative-philology document for understanding the Northwest-Semitic background of the Hebrew Bible. Chapter 1 covers KTU 1.1 + 1.2 — Baʿlu vs Yammu — including: the assembly of the gods; Yammu's demand for tribute; the messengers' arrival; the duel; Baʿlu's victory with weapons made by Kothar-wa-Khasis the divine craftsman; the proclamation of Baʿlu's kingship. The text is severely fragmentary in places — KTU 1.1 has only column iv substantially preserved (~28 lines), and KTU 1.2 column ii is broken away entirely. Lacunae are marked per the project's lacuna-bracket convention.

The Baal Cycle, KTU 1.1 + 1.2 — Baʿlu vs Yammu: the storm-god's conflict with Sea

Standard ʾIlu epithet-cluster: ṯr ʾil 'Bull ʾIlu' + lṭpn 'the Benevolent One' + ḥtk 'patriarch'. The bull-theriomorphism is the Northwest-Semitic head-of-pantheon imagery (central entry bull-of-el-thr-ilu-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible-bull-of-jacob, claim_type inferred since the Hebrew ʾăbîr Yaʿăqōb cognation is well-attested but theological-historical inheritance is a scholarly reconstruction rather than explicit in either source-text). The Ugaritic vocalization ʾIlu is preserved per project policy (central entry el-ugaritic-ilu-northwest-semitic-pantheon-head-cross-corpus).

Notes Verse 19

Opening of the pacification-oracle qryy b ʾarṣ mlḥmt / rm ddym sk šlm / ʾarbdd l kbd šdm 'place war in the earth; pour peace into the midst; tranquility into the midst of the fields'. The ddym lexeme is contested — 'love-tokens' (Pardee 2003, default here), 'mandrakes' (Gibson 1978; cf. Hebrew dûdāʾîm Gen 30:14), or 'mounds, hills' (Ginsberg 1955). Possible Hebrew Bible echo in the Isa 2:4 / Mic 4:3 swords-into-plowshares peace-oracle, though the parallels are typological rather than philologically cognate.

Notes Verse 1

Kothar-wa-Khasis's Mediterranean-Egyptian abode: Kaphtor (= Crete; Ugaritic kptr) for his throne, Memphis (Ugaritic ḥkpt, from Egyptian Hwt-kꜢ-Ptḥ 'House of the soul of Ptah') for his land of inheritance. The geography situates the divine craftsman in the Late Bronze Age metal-and-glass-working centers; see central entry kothar-wa-khasis-divine-craftsman-cross-corpus-speech-act-weapon-naming.

Notes Verse 13

The famous mystery-revelation formula rgm ʿṣ w lḫšt ʾabn — a fixed Ugaritic liturgical-formula for esoteric cosmic-communication. Smith 1994 vol 1 reads as fixed formula; Ginsberg 1955 reads more concretely as 'message of timber and stone'. Cross-corpus echo at Hab 2:11 (stone-and-timber crying out) and Ps 19:1-4 (heavens' speech). Central entry word-of-tree-whisper-of-stone-mystery-revelation-formula-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible covers (promoted from overlay at ch 2 Editor pass when formula recurred at KTU 1.3-iii).

ʿnn ʾilm literally 'cloud-attendants of the gods' — divine messenger-class with cloud-traveling associations (ʿnn 'cloud'). Surface translation generalizes to 'attendants of the gods' to avoid pre-resolving the cloud-attendant register onto the later rkb ʿrpt 'Rider of the Clouds' epithet of Baʿlu (KTU 1.2-iv:6) or onto NT 'coming on clouds' Christology. The bn ʾilm / divine-assembly context governs the line (central entry bn-ilm-sons-of-god-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bnei-elohim).

Notes Verse 14

The YW line — the single most-contested Ugaritic-Hebrew comparative-philology data-point. ʾIlu names a son YW (Ugaritic yw) at the divine banquet preceding Yammu's exaltation. Three named-scholarship readings on the YHWH-connection question: (a) de Moor 1971 reads YW as a real divine name, likely YHWH-related; (b) Cross 1973 is cautiously open; (c) Smith 1994 vol 1, pp. 152-160, is the most cautious — reads YW as one of ʾIlu's seventy sons being named, with the YHWH connection 'possible but not proven'. The Editor preserves bare transliteration YW with no vocalization-commitment. This line does NOT prove that Yahweh originated as a Canaanite deity; the philological evidence is genuinely contested. Central entry yw-line-ktu-1-1-iv-14-proto-yahweh-candidate-cross-corpus-ugaritic documents all three readings.

Yammu's elevation is performatively-enacted by ʾIlu's speech-act-naming.

Notes Verse 24

ʾIlu's kingship-deposition decree against Baʿlu. The throne-deposition formula grš … l ksʾi mlkh shares vocabulary with Isa 14:13 (Helal ben Shahar's deposition); Ezek 28 (Tyre); Ps 89:5. The verb grš 'drive out' is the same root as Yagrush ('Let-him-drive-out'), the weapon Kothar will later forge at 1.2-iv:12; it is also the verb of the Eden expulsion (Gen 3:24 va-y'garesh et ha-adam), but the Editor preserves 'drive him out' as the literal default rather than the Eden-resonant 'cast him out' to avoid pre-resolving the Gen 3 typology.

[KTU 1.2 col i: opening lines fragmentary. The scene that unfolds: Yammu (the Sea-god) dispatches his two messengers (mlʾakm) to the divine assembly (pḫr mʿd) at Mount Lel, demanding the surrender of Baʿlu. ʾIlu and the gods abjectly submit; Baʿlu rages and must be restrained by ʿAnatu and ʿAṯtartu.]

Notes Verse 11

First clear occurrence of Yammu in the surviving text. The lemma mlʾak 'messenger' is the etymological source of Hebrew malʾāk (also 'angel') and ultimately Greek angelos. Surface renders as 'messenger' (neutral); the 'angel' gloss would risk anachronism in this Bronze Age divine-political context.

Notes Verse 12

ṯpṭ nhr 'Judge Naharu (= River)' — Yammu's binomial partner-name in standing parallelism Yammu // Naharu. The Yam/Nahar (Sea/River) doublet is itself a major comparative-mythology marker: cf. Hab 3:8 ha-b-naharim charah YHWH … ʿal ha-yam ʿevratekha matching exactly the Ugaritic yam//naharim doubling. The ṯpṭ 'Judge' title (cognate to Hebrew šōpēṭ) marks the judicial-royal authority claim Yammu makes against Baʿlu.

pḫr mʿd 'gathered assembly' — the formal designation for the divine council at Mount Lel. Cross-corpus to Akkadian puḫru ša ilāni (Adapa, Enuma Elish) and to Hebrew sod YHWH / ʿădat ʾēl / ʿădat qĕdōshîm (Ps 89:8; Ps 82:1; Ps 89:6). The cluster is among the most-foundational cross-corpus divine-assembly attestations. Central entry divine-council-phr-mad-cross-corpus-ugaritic-akkadian-hebrew-bible (Mullen 1980; Heiser 2015; Cross 1973).

Notes Verse 21

MAJOR cross-corpus to Hebrew bĕnê (hā)ʾĕlōhîm (Gen 6:2, 4; Job 1:6, 2:1, 38:7; Ps 29:1, 89:7; Deut 32:8 LXX/4QDeut^j) and to qĕdōshîm 'holy ones' in divine-council contexts (Ps 89:6-8; Job 5:1; 15:15; Zech 14:5). Central entry bn-ilm-sons-of-god-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bnei-elohim. The entry's rationale documents the explicit disavowal of the WoH-Watchers-engineering reading of the Gen 6:2 / 1 Enoch material.

THE central epithet of Baʿlu. rkb ʿrpt 'Rider of the Clouds' — MANDATORY cross-corpus with Hebrew Ps 68:5 rōkēb bā-ʿărābôt, Deut 33:26 rōkēb šāmayim, Ps 18:11 (YHWH-on-cherub-rides), Ps 104:3 (clouds-as-chariot), Isa 19:1. The Hebrew tradition's reassignment of Baʿlu's storm-theophany to Yahweh is the textually clearest case of Baʿlu-epithet-absorption into Yahwistic theology (Cross 1973; Day 2000). Central entry rider-of-the-clouds-rkb-arpt-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible-storm-theophany — entry's rationale explicitly disavows Christological pre-resolution onto Dan 7:13 / Mark 14:62 / Rev 1:7.

Central entry yagrush-ayamur-speech-act-named-divine-weapons-cross-corpus; speech-act-efficacy thesis at speech-act-efficacy-language-power-of-life-and-death-cross-corpus.

The closing line. tgʿrm picks up the same gʿr 'rebuke' verb Baʿlu used against the cowering gods at 1.2-i:25 — the same lexeme as Hebrew gāʿar of YHWH's rebuke of the sea (Ps 18:15; 104:7; Isa 17:13; Nah 1:4). ʿAṯtartu's rebuke seals Baʿlu's victory and parallels the Hebrew YHWH-rebukes-sea pattern. Reading of b šm is contested: 'by name' (incantation; default here), 'with shame' (Pardee 2003 alternative), 'as for the name' (Smith 1994).

Notes Verse 1

First mention of the famous window-debate that returns at KTU 1.4-vi:11-15 and KTU 1.4-vii:13-30. Ugaritic ʾurbt 'lattice, skylight' is the direct cognate of Hebrew ʾărubbāh 'window of heaven' (Gen 7:11; 8:2; Mal 3:10). The Hebrew Bible's ʾărubbôt ha-šāmayim cluster preserves the Northwest-Semitic cosmic-window cosmology (Day 2000; Smith & Pitard 2009 vol 2 pp. 612-624).

Notes Verse 22

Construction order from Baʿlu to Kothar. bhtm tbnn // hklm trmmn 'palaces shall be built / temples shall be erected' opens the construction-sequence of KTU 1.4. The verbs bny 'build' (cognate to Hebrew bānāh) and rwm 'erect' (cognate to Hebrew rûm) anchor the typology.

[KTU 1.4 col i: a transition-column. The opening describes the absence of a palace befitting Baʿlu, repeating elements of the earlier complaint. The column then narrates the preparation of gifts (precious metals) for ʾAṯirat, who must intercede with ʾIlu. KTU 1.4 is the longest single tablet of the Cycle (~410 lines across 8 columns).]

Notes Verse 16

ʾAṯirat's standing epithet qnyt ʾilm 'Creatress of the gods' — the shared NW-Semitic creator-vocabulary cluster. Direct philological cognate to Hebrew Gen 14:19, 22 qōnēh šāmayim wā-ʾāreṣ 'Creator of heaven and earth' (Melchizedek's formula). The Hebrew tradition re-allocates the qōnēh creator-title from ʾAṯirat/ʿElyôn to YHWH-El. Day 2000 pp. 39-41; Smith 2001 pp. 47-49.

Notes Verse 55

Lebanese cedars (Cedrus libani) — the Late Bronze / Iron Age prestige construction-wood, supplied along the Eastern Mediterranean trade-economy. Historical-economic continuity with 1 Kgs 5:6-10 (Hiram of Tyre supplies cedars to Solomon). Not typological parallelism but shared regional construction-material economy (Liphschitz 2007; Hurowitz 1992).

[KTU 1.4 col vi: Kothar-wa-Khasis arrives at Baʿlu's Ṣapunu and begins the construction of the palace. Baʿlu personally directs the work; cedar, silver, gold and lapis-lazuli are gathered. The fire-firing of the palace (the architectural-firing of mud-brick) takes seven days. Cosmic-temple-building parallels with 1 Kgs 5-8 (Solomon's temple), Ezek 40-48 (the visionary temple), Exod 25-31, 35-40 (the tabernacle). See Hurowitz 1992.]

Notes Verse 11

The famous window-debate (KTU 1.4-vi:11-15 + vii:13-30): Kothar proposes a window; Baʿlu first refuses (cosmological worry about Yammu seeing in); then reverses (vii:28). Ugaritic ʾurbt 'lattice' is the direct cognate of Hebrew ʾărubbāh in the ʾărubbôt ha-šāmayim 'windows of heaven' cluster (Gen 7:11; 8:2; Mal 3:10). The window is the cosmological aperture through which the storm-god's voice issues.

THE central theophany-passage of the Baal Cycle. ytn qlh b ʿrpt // qdš tr ʾarṣ 'he gives forth his voice in the clouds // (his) holy (voice) shakes the earth'. F. M. Cross's flagship case: Hebrew Ps 29 (the seven-fold qol YHWH) is a Yahwehized Baʿlu hymn. Cross-corpus to Ps 29; Ps 18:13-14 // 2 Sam 22:14-15; Hab 3:3-15; Job 37:2-5; Jer 25:30; Joel 4:16. Cross 1973 pp. 151-156; Day 2000.

First introduction of Môtu (Death personified) — proleptic to the conflict that unfolds in KTU 1.5-1.6 (chapter 3). Ugaritic mt is the direct cognate of Hebrew māwet 'death'; the personified form is preserved in Hebrew poetic-prophetic attestations (Hos 13:14; Isa 25:8; Hab 2:5). [KTU 1.4 col viii: with the palace complete, Baʿlu now sends his messengers Gpn-wa-Ugar to Môtu (Death personified) in the underworld. This proleptic challenge sets up the conflict that occupies Chapter 3 (KTU 1.5-1.6) of the Translation. Back · Library

Contents

    Wheel of Heaven is an open, multilingual reading of the ancient world's creation traditions — Raëlian, biblical, Mesopotamian, and others — through a single working hypothesis: that the beings called Elohim were a small advanced human civilization that came here, designed life on Earth, and left a record in the religious texts. The reading runs across twelve ages of the precessional cycle, from the project's beginning twenty-two thousand years ago to the present age of disclosure and into the long future the next Great Year is opening. The site is free, source-aware, and built so the work can be checked.
